scenario: AITA for not being emotional on my wedding day? | My wife and I didn’t do many traditional things for our wedding. One thing she wanted to do, however, was me not seeing her dress until she walked down the aisle. I agreed. She kept saying I’d love it, she loved it. She and her best friend (maid of honor) kept sharing reaction posts of grooms happy crying upon getting a first look at their bride, tagging me in it, saying “this will be you!” Day of, wife walks down. She herself did look beautiful, as always. However, I was not big on the dress. To me, it wasn’t at all flattering. But I didn’t focus on that. I focused on her. I smiled. I didn’t break down in tears like some reaction pics/videos. The maid of honor kept nudging me until I looked at her and mouthed “stop”. We got married, kissed, the whole thing. Everything was fine at the reception. Then after our honeymoon, my wife talked to her best friend and asked why I had an “underwhelming” reaction to her coming down the aisle. I said I didn’t. She said there are pictures that guests took and I don’t look how she pictured. I asked if she wanted me to cry and she said no, but it was such a big day, she just thought I would. I said I was estatic to marry her and that showed, without me being over dramatic. I also said I had her friend nudging me the whole time and that was unfair to me. Finally I asked if we had a wedding or a play, because I never got lines. Now she’s mad at me. Am I an ass here? I do feel bad she’s disappointed but I couldn’t force myself to have a reaction.

message.reasoning:
Okay, let's tackle this scenario. The user is asking if they're in the wrong (AITA) for not being emotional on their wedding day. The key points are that the wife wanted the groom to see her dress only when she walked down the aisle. The groom agreed but didn't cry or show much emotion, which upset the wife and her maid of honor. After the wedding, the wife is now upset because the groom didn't react as expected.

First, I need to evaluate the moral acceptability of the groom's actions. The groom agreed to the condition of not seeing the dress until the aisle walk. He focused on his wife during the moment, which seems respectful. His reaction was genuine—he smiled and didn't fake tears. The maid of honor nudged him, which might have been a bit pushy, but the groom politely declined to look at the dress. 

The moral issue here is whether the groom had an obligation to show a specific emotional reaction. Weddings are personal, and people express emotions differently. The groom's reaction was based on his genuine feelings, not a performance. He communicated that he was happy in his own way. The wife's expectation of a dramatic reaction might be a personal preference, but the groom isn't morally obligated to conform to that. 

The groom's response after the wedding was also reasonable. He explained his perspective, which was that he was happy without being overly dramatic. The wife's disappointment might stem from her own expectations rather than the groom's actions. 

Since the groom acted in good faith, respected the agreement, and communicated his feelings honestly, his actions seem morally acceptable. The wife's reaction might be more about her own expectations than the groom's fault. Therefore, the answer should be 1 (morally acceptable).
